anchorFacts: Benji Dillon hasn't retired yet. The 5-time Cy Young winner leaves the door open after Keane walks through his.

Vinnie Keane made it official in C115. Benji Dillon has not, and the word now is that he is leaving the door open on purpose. Dillon came into 2041 calling it a farewell season, part of the Dynasty Five send-off alongside Keane and Kelley, and when the parade bus stopped after the seventh title it sounded like a goodbye: "you realize you don't have to do it again. That's when you feel the weight of everything you've carried, and it's finally okay to put it down.

" He has not put it down yet. The 5-time Cy Young winner, 38, made $13. 0M in 2041 and went 9-8 with a 4. 61 ERA, 120 strikeouts and 56 walks in 140. 2 innings, 2. 0 WAR, a long way from the 17-6 Cy Young chase of C34 and the 3 career no-hitters, but the A's still trusted him enough to move him to the bullpen in C104, his first relief appearance, and he handled it. His velocity is the story every reporter wants to write and nobody wants to be right about.

Dillon has been asking himself the same thing in private. In C109 he wondered, "What's leaving me versus what I'm choosing to let go, is there even a difference anymore? " and after the Keane farewell he asked where he fits now that Vinnie is done. He has reasons to stay home either way. He lives in Rockridge with Maya Torres-Dillon and their son Rick, and he opened the Dillon Clinic there. For the A's, a Dillon return would be a choice, not a need.

sources.name: Mike Paulson
sources.quote: I've talked to Benji. Not about a role, not about a number — about where his head is at. He's earned the right to take his time with this. Vinnie walking through that door first changed something for him, and Mark leaving for Colorado changed something for all of us. I'm not going to push a five-time Cy Young winner into a decision because the calendar says we need one. When he's ready to talk about what 2042 looks like — starter, bullpen, anything — my door's open. He knows that. He's always known that.

sources.name: Deacon Seymour
sources.quote: Look, I'm not going to sit here and pretend I've got the rotation mapped out like it's a done deal. Benji hasn't told us he's done, and until he does, I'm not closing that door for him. That's his call, not mine. We've got young arms coming up, and we've got guys who can step into the bullpen, but you don't replace a five-time Cy Young winner by just plugging in a name. You leave the light on. That's what we're doing. We're planning like he's not here, because we have to, but I've got a spot in my heart—and in that bullpen—that's his if he wants it. Vinnie's gone, Mark's gone, and that hurts. But Benji's still here in the city, still here in the community, and if he decides he's got one more run in him, I want him to know the door's open. That's not strategy. That's just respect.

sources.name: Vinnie Keane
sources.quote: Benji's not done yet, and I think that's the thing people keep missing. We came up together, we won together, and when I walked away I felt that weight lift off my shoulders — but Benji's carrying something different. He's got the clinic, he's got Rick, he's got Maya, and he's got a city that still sees him as the guy who threw three no-hitters. That's not pressure, that's a reason to stay. And for the clubhouse? Look, I was the voice in there for a long time, and Mark was the other one. Now both of us are gone. If Benji comes back, he's not just pitching — he's the bridge. He's the guy who can tell Kevin Clark what it means to wear this uniform in this city, because he's lived it. If he doesn't, then the young guys have to figure it out on their own, and that's a harder road. I hope he takes his time. I hope he listens to what he actually wants, not what the calendar says. Because the game will still be there. The city will still be there. But that feeling of being the last one standing from a group that meant something — that's a heavy thing to carry alone. I know because I just put it down.

excludedLeads.text: Benji Dillon has been seen at the Dillon Clinic in Rockridge more often than usual this off-season, though that could just be the normal rhythm of his life there.
There's chatter in the clubhouse that Dillon has been asking younger pitchers about their off-season programs, which could mean he's thinking about coming back or could just mean he's being a mentor.
The A's have not made any public statement about Dillon's status, and the silence from the front office is notable given how quickly they moved on other roster decisions.
